lessons.title: One hypothesis
lessons.why: Bundled changes teach nothing and make rollback impossible.
body: Write one sentence: what you think is wrong, what you will change, what evidence would prove it. Change that thing. Collect the same Call-ID style evidence again. Then decide.

A reboot plus a dial-plan edit plus a firewall change is how an outage ends with no one knowing why. The evidence pack is the Call-ID, the effective policy, the ladder, and the CQD or Call Analytics row that matches the scope.
lessons.say: One hypothesis, one change, one evidence pack.
lessons.fault: Three vendors change three boxes and the call works for an unknown reason.
lessons.listen: Change one thing at a time, and keep the Call-ID with the result.

lessons.title: Reading a ladder
lessons.why: The response code is the branch. A story without codes is not a diagnosis.
body: Order the messages. INVITE, 100, 180 or 183, 200, ACK, then later BYE. 183 is early media, not an answer. 488 means the SDP was refused. 408 means something did not answer in time. 503 means the hop is refusing service. 487 often means the caller cancelled.
Join on Call-ID. Two calls that start in the same second are not the same call. Read the first non-success on the hop that sent it, then stop. Do not restart a healthy SBC because a 180 felt slow.
lessons.say: I read the first failing response on one Call-ID.
lessons.fault: Two captures are compared and they are different calls.
lessons.listen: Follow one Call-ID. 183 is not an answer. 488 is codecs. 503 is a hop refusing work.

lessons.title: Call Analytics
lessons.why: One user, one call. That is the scope of this tool.
depends: A support role that can open it
body: Call Analytics shows the streams of a user’s call: jitter, loss, round-trip, and the client. Use it when one person suffered and the building did not. The Teams Communications Support Engineer role is the troubleshooting role people usually mean here. Check the current role article.
A building-wide problem hunted one user at a time will take a week. Switch tools when the scope changes.

lessons.fault: A site problem is debugged as twenty separate user tickets.
lessons.listen: Use Call Analytics for one user’s call. Use CQD when the building is the question.

lessons.title: Call Quality Dashboard
lessons.why: CQD is how you see a subnet. It is only as honest as the building map.
body: CQD aggregates streams by dimensions such as subnet and user agent. Separate jitter, loss, and round-trip in your head. High jitter with DSCP 0 suggests a mark that never survived. High loss with EF still set suggests a congested or dirty link. Long RTT with almost no loss suggests distance or a hairpin.
If the VPN pool is labeled headquarters, headquarters looks terrible and the real LAN is fine. Fix the map before you present the dashboard. Power BI on top of CQD inherits the same map.

lessons.title: Trunk health
lessons.why: A down trunk is not a dial-plan problem.
body: Look at SBC status in the Teams admin center and at the SBC’s OPTIONS log. If TLS failed, stop. Certificate name, expiry, and chain come before regex. If OPTIONS succeed and one number fails, then you have earned the right to open the dial plan.
SIP Tester language shows up in operations chatter. Use the health view and a real test call. Do not invent a hidden tester result you did not run.

chart.title: Order of looks
chart.note: Do not start at the dial plan.

lessons.say: I check TLS and OPTIONS before I touch a normalization rule.
lessons.fault: The dial plan is rewritten while the certificate is expired.
lessons.listen: Trunk health first: certificate, OPTIONS, admin-center status. Then the dial plan.

lessons.title: A fault catalog
lessons.why: Naming the fault is the skill. The tools are how you prove the name.
body: Silence after 200 is media ports or SRTP. 488 is codecs. A single remote user with DSCP 0 is often the VPN. A building with loss and EF intact is the link. A number that never leaves Teams is normalization or policy. A queue that does not answer is a resource account, agents, or overflow.
Emergency failures are their own catalog: wrong route, missing location, stripped PIDF-LO, notification not assigned. Do not file them under ‘audio quality.’
lessons.say: I can sort a symptom into signaling, media, policy, or location before I pick a tool.
lessons.fault: Every ticket is labeled ‘Teams down’ and none of them are the same fault.
lessons.listen: Sort the fault first: signaling, media, policy, or emergency location. Then open the matching tool.
